utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Happy New Year to everybody. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ninkovic, for coming back. We will now continue and hopefully complete your testimony before the end of tomorrow. Cross-examination by the Prosecution continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well come back, Mr. Ninkovic. There are a couple of topics that I want to return to, topics that I questioned you about last year in December. One of them was the issue of the Crisis Staff doing something about Lugar's actions at Crkvina, namely the killing of 15 or 16 people. I asked you if Lugar -- I asked you about sending of letters, doing something, doing anything at all, and you said that nothing could be done because -- particularly by Dr. Blagoje Simic because that would have placed his life in jeopardy. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, like that, but I can repeat what I said. Lugar was a member of the army. He was authorised to process that crime that happened [as interpreted]. The military bodies were there, the military police, the investigative organs of the army, the military prosecutor were there. See, if this man had killed 15 people, another victim more would mean nothing to him. It is certain that that man would carry out an act of reprisal against Blagoje Simic had he informed higher authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's how I understood your evidence. There was one aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. If I could just ask for a clarification page 1, line 25 and page 2, line number 1. Mr. Ninkovic, the translation says Lugar was a member of the army, full stop. He was authorised to process that crime that happened. I just don't understand what he was authorised to process that crime that happened means and I don't know who the he was. If you could clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that. I said the army was authorised to process that, the bodies of the army, the military police, the military prosecution, because he was a member of the army. He was a criminal and he didn't have any such authorities, particularly after this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was however a singular lack of action on the part of the army in doing anything, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When the 1st Krajina Corps came to that region with their large military formations which in a way placed the area of Samac under their area of responsibility in the military sense, then the processing process began and that was when the military prosecution in Banja Luka initiated proceedings against Lugar, Crni and perhaps some others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but that had nothing to do with the massacre at Crkvina, that had everything to do with their role in the closure of the Posavina corridor. That was the situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely the contents of the indictment -- the indictment. Because I didn't see it, but what I know is that he was accused of several crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you saying that he was accused of the crime at Crkvina, amongst other crimes, namely the murder of 15 or 16 civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the investigation was conducted in that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Well, we'll return to that in just a moment but let me direct your attention to another feature of the evidence from last month. I asked you this question and you gave this answer. Question: Are you saying that something like D62/1 could never have been sent because if Lugar and his associates had discovered such a complaint, Dr. Blagoje Simic's life would have been in danger? Answer: I wish to say precisely that. Namely, if they -- they were to find out that Dr. Blagoje Simic had complained to someone who was more powerful and above him, then his life would have been in danger. Do you remember me asking you that question and you giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember but I think that there is a small misunderstanding here. The investigation was conducted by the 1st Krajina Corps and not by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you a very simple issue. If Dr. Blagoje Simic had complained to someone about the Crkvina massacre, your position is that Lugar and his associates would have placed his life in danger?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do I take it from that answer, then, that there was a perception at least on your part, that Lugar acted in company with a number of other men when he was carrying out activities such as the Crkvina massacre, a number of other paramilitaries? That there was a gang of them, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was an isolated act, that's what I believe about this event. It was an isolated act by Lugar and I believe that it has nothing to do with others but in that group of volunteers, there were certainly people who did have a predilection towards crime but I think that that particular crime, which was very cruel, and I wish to express my sympathy to the families of the victims, I believe that it was an isolated event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said quite clearly last year that if Dr. Blagoje Simic had done anything about the event at Crkvina, his life would have been in danger. Do you mean by that that you know of something that he did to consider -- do you know -- let me rephrase that. Do you mean by that that you know that he thought about the issue, talked about the issue, discussed the issue, considered alternatives?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that Dr. Blagoje Simic thought about this. I know that he was afraid of Lugar, not only Lugar but of some other people from that group, and based on my knowledge that he was afraid of them, especially of Lugar, I said that Blagoje Simic's life would be in danger had he informed higher authorities, because Lugar had killed 15 people and one more victim would have meant nothing to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever actually hear or see or have reported to you anything that Dr. Blagoje Simic had said about taking some action in respect of the massacre at Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories about that event only later, when the 1st Krajina Corps arrived in the area. This was discussed more openly only then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, your position last year in December when you gave evidence about this, was that all that you ever heard were really rumours and you didn't even find out about it until much later. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not quite correct. I said that I didn't find out about the event immediately after it happened, but I found out about it once the units of the 1st Krajina Corps arrived, and this was at the end of June, 1992. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me remind you of what you said. I'll read the passage to you. This was in answer to questions from Mr. Pantelic. He asked you about the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, could we have a page? MR. DI FAZIO: 13531.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Answer: No, I don't know anything about this, there was no official report or information about that. Question: All right. Was this talked about among the population? Answer: A bit later there was some talk but all of it was hearsay. There was a war going on. There is a lot of misinformation going on during a war, so the story about this crime was something that could -- that I could neither believe nor disbelieve. Question: Can you tell me when in which period, you heard these rumours. Answer: This is considerably later. You gave the impression there didn't you that all you ever knew about Crkvina was some rumour and that that was not until much later. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I received more relevant information only upon the arrival of the 1st Krajina Corps, and this fits in with what I said in response to a question by Mr. Pantelic, but it's true that there were no -- there was no official information. I didn't see it. I didn't hear anything about it. There were rumours but rumours were rampant about different topics, and I will repeat in war it's difficult to know what is true and what is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that taking some action in respect of this incident was a matter that would have been of the utmost concern to the Crisis Staff? And I say that notwithstanding your assertion that jurisdiction over the crime rested with the military. Regardless of that, it was still a matter that the Crisis Staff would have given the utmost importance to and would have been seriously concerned or should have been seriously concerned about following up?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at it from the aspect that this crime happened in the territory of the municipality of Samac where the Crisis Staff had certain authority, absolutely, in that sense, the Crisis Staff should have reviewed that question, looked at it, and initiated some activities but I repeat, if they had the relevant information, a report, facts, then it could have relevantly discussed that, and offer up some kind of initiative, but this was actually something that was in the jurisdiction of the military organs so it was in the military domain to arrest such a man, to conduct the investigative proceedings, to issue an indictment for the murders. These things should have been carried out by the military bodies and they should have informed the Crisis Staff about this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the police, Todorovic, Savo Cancarevic having any knowledge about the events at Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to have known that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was nothing then to prevent them telling the Crisis Staff of what had taken place?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the police first of all should have prevented this from happening, this Lugar should not have been allowed to enter the detention area with weapons, and because he attempted to do that, the police should have prevented him from doing so. So that was the first failure. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P127, the 13 signatories document. I assume we have the B/C/S version for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document your familiar with, having already seen it earlier in your testimony. Just for the sake of speed, you'll see that the document is divided up into paragraphs and the text refers to the number of the paragraphs. On page 2 of the English version, so it may be somewhere around there in the B/C/S, and in the fifth paragraph there is a reference to this episode. I just want to read a passage to you so can you please find the fifth -- the fifth paragraph? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The passage that I want to read to you is very short. "The crime committed by Lugar in Crkvina was reported on by Yugoslav and international press and attributed to Serbian soldiers from our municipality creating a difficult collective legacy that will have to be cleared up only after the war." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. I have the passage, "The Special Forces who came to train." I found that passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's the fifth paragraph. Do you have that? Definitely the fifth paragraph. No number. The text itself says "fifth" and it's on -- I can't tell you where on the B/C/S it is, but in the English it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it. It's on page 2 at the bottom of the page, about the specials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And about halfway through the paragraph, it talks about -- starts to talk about massive arrests and isolation of Croats and Muslims and then that passage that I read to you appears. Do you now have it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it. It's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with the assessment of the authors of this document that the crime committed in Crkvina was reported on in the Yugoslav and international press?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information, as far as I know, was compiled on the 1st of December, 1992, so at the end of the year. So this is about six or seven months after the crime. I don't know whether the Yugoslav or the international press wrote about it, because I didn't have access to such information at that time. It's possible that they did. But they probably wrote about that later, perhaps in the autumn or something like that, but I'm certain that they did not report about it after the event itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked with the press, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the period, as I said, until I was appointed to my post in the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that was during 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning of the war until, let's say the beginning of July, I was performing duties regarding media and information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now that would have placed you in a very good position to keep abreast of reporting of events in which you yourself were caught up, sorry to interrupt, particularly in the Yugoslavian press at least, if not the international press?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] As I said, in that period immediately after the event, there was no official report. My superior, who was in charge of the media and information sphere was not able to make or compile a relevant information for the media. I assume that in this period that you're talking about, reports were being written about this event only later, after Lugar, Crni and other volunteers had left this area. After processing in Banja Luka, then some information was released to the public regarding these volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is dated December, 1992 and it seems to contemplate reporting having taken place in the international and Yugoslav press so presumably there was some reporting at the very least before December of 1992, if this document is correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot judge or talk about this act, and I cannot tell what the author of this article -- document meant, so the person who wrote the document should be asked about it. If we look at the document, it was written by the body for morale in the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. I told you that as far as this information is concerned, this information is not quite proper, because it deals with civilian issues, which are not in the domain of military authorities. Looking at the information as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not interested in demarcation of what is proper sphere of activity of the civilian or military authorities. What I'm interested in is a very simple issue. This event at Crkvina was, I put to you and I suggest to you, a matter that was known almost immediately throughout the municipality of Bosanski Samac, was known to just about everyone in the municipality and I suggest it must have been known to you as well, and it was met with complete inactivity on the part of the civilian authorities. They did absolutely nothing following -- they did nothing to arrest Lugar, they did nothing to cajole or encourage others to arrest Lugar, they took absolutely no steps at all, and I suggest to you that that is the truth of the case and you know it. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you that everybody knew. How do you mean everybody knew? How can tens of thousands of people know what happened in Crkvina one night? How can they know that? That claim of yours cannot stand. It's quite understandable that we cannot accept something like that. Only the authorised bodies could know about it and they are the ones who are responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I suggest to you that knowledge of the event was widespread in Bosanski Samac and the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, yes, but not right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio, I wonder again just for clarification, sake, on page 9, lines 23 and 24, Mr. Ninkovic mentions "after processing in Banja Luka, then some information was released to the public regarding these volunteers." I would be interested to know what after processing in Banja Luka means. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, and if I may respectfully add another aspect to Your Honour's question, perhaps the witness could also ask what that information was that was released after the Banja Luka trial. Sorry, do you understand the question that Her Honour raised and the question that I added on to it, tacked on to it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that after Lugar and Crni were processed, I think that somebody else was on that list too, after that, some information appeared in public, and they were more freely exchanged among the population, among citizens, et cetera. I have not read any official report of the prosecutor with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information can you recall being released after the Banja Luka trial?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information of the following type: That these volunteers went beyond the framework of the law, that they acted arbitrarily, apart from military hierarchy and the military does not suffer arbitrariness gladly. So only assignments given through a hierarchy are to be carried out and that in this way the system of command and control had been infringed upon due to the arbitrary behaviour of the persons that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were from the area and had lived in the area of Bosanski Samac all your life, basically. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Samac but I lived in the area of the municipality of Odzak, but from 1987 until the present day, I have been living in Samac, rather working in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic, he was a man who also had strong roots and had lived basically all his life in Bosanski Samac, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born in Novi Grad. I don't know when he moved to Samac but I know that he has been in Samac for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Tadic was interviewed by officers of the Office of the Prosecutor in March of 1998 and he was asked about the state of knowledge in the community of the Crkvina massacre and he had this to say and I'll just quote to you what he said. He was talking about Crkvina, okay? Question by the then investigator: I know that this killing was widely known by people in the area --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to my colleague, if he we can have a page? MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly, I'm referring to the old interviews, it's Exhibit P139, page 7 of that interview. P139, page 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Question: I know that this killing was widely known by people in the area and I assume that this was brought to your attention. Answer by Mr. Tadic: Yes, it could not have been avoided not to hear about it. Even housewives who had spent the war in cellars heard about it. That was something unimaginable at that time that somebody would commit such a crime for no apparent reason. And that obviously placed a terrible shadow over all the relationships in Samac. Now, he is essentially saying there that this was -- what had happened in Crkvina was a matter of notoriety. Do you have any idea why it is that he asserts that it was a matter of some notoriety and yet you heard nothing but rumours and only then not until much later after the event?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement of Mr. Tadic that even housewives knew about this is inconsistent at any rate but it's also a bit strange. I assert that in that part, his statement is inconsistent. I will agree, though, with the part of the statement in which he says that this is undoubtedly a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to finish up on this topic, the Banja Luka trial that we've raised from time to time in the course of your evidence took place only after Lugar and others had been arrested by the military. That's the logical sequence, isn't it, arrest first and then at some later point the trial?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are regular proceedings that are instituted any way. Are you talking about this in principle or are you referring to this specific event?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the specific event but let me -- I don't want to get bogged down in unnecessary detail. Let me get straight to the point. When Lugar came to be arrested the military had no problems in arresting him and dealing with him, locking him up and dealing with him, that's the case, isn't it? It wasn't the case that they were terrified of acting against him or moving against him, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep repeating the same thing to you. It is only when a big mighty military formation came in, and I will remind you that the 1st Krajina Corps had half of the Army of Republika Srpska in its ranks and General Talic was the second person in command in the Army of Republika Srpska. It is only then that this could have been carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what you're telling the Chamber, is it? Nothing could work against Lugar, no one could take any action, it wasn't until you had the massed force of, as you say, half the Army of the Republika Srpska with General Talic in command that finally something could be done about Lugar? That's your position? That's what you're telling these Judges? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that the Crisis Staff could not have done all of that. That is to say prosecute the persons involved, arrest them, et cetera. The command of the second Posavina Brigade could though, but now why they didn't do it, that is the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to another topic now. One of the other topics that was raised last December was the issue of the executive board that didn't function in the first part of 1992. Do you recall that I asked you questions about that? And that you said that the executive board only started to function in June of 1992? I'm talking about the executive board of the -- of the Crisis Staff. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You asked me about who was on the executive board and you asked me about executive -- about the Official Gazette, where my name is mentioned. I told you that this executive board did not function, it did not meet, and sometime in June, an executive council started functioning presided by Milan Simic, the vice-president was Mirko Lukic and sometime in the autumn more people were included in this council. That is to say Veselin Blagojevic, I think, and Milos Pavlovic, the first one being in charge of housing and the other one in charge of social services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. It's your assertion that it didn't start to function until June of 1992 that I'm interested in. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P124?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ninkovic, the way these gazettes are laid out is somewhat confusing but I'll do my best to direct you to the portions that I'm interested in in the B/C/S version. And if Your Honours please, page 12 of the English version. Firstly, this - you agree, I think - is the Official Gazette? It's for year 1, edition number 1, put out in June of 1994, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, at page 12 of the English, and as part of what I think is paragraph 3 of the gazette, it deals with a decision on the election of members of the executive council. Can you see if you can find that in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 12 in the document that I have are the contents of this Official Gazette. I can't find this. If you're talking about page 12 I have the contents there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I was only --

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please tell me what the actual name of the decision involved is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's decision on the election of members of the executive council, and it lists a whole -- it's got a whole list of names, your name included as deputy secretary of the municipal secretariat of national defence. It's got Todorovic's name there. Do you see all of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. It's on page 7 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, it says that there was a session on the 28th of March, 1992, and the municipal assembly decided to elect these people on to the executive council and that's where your name appears. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your position is that this was a non-functioning executive council, it didn't work?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 1 deals with members of the council. Go to Article 2, please. You see that it says that "The President of the executive council, together with various other people, is charged, is given the job of, carrying out preparations for the transition to work under wartime conditions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a very important task, is it not, that the executive council was given?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will now go back to this Official Gazette a bit. It was published on the 3rd of June, 1994. I don't know exactly how this Official Gazette was printed. I'm expressing a certain doubt, suspicion that is, that some decisions were entered subsequently into this gazette but that's not that important. I want to say that this executive council did not operate. I was never invited to attend any meetings of this executive council. As a matter of fact, no one even talked to me about the actual composition of this executive council. Then also, this is a very short period, from the end of March until the beginning of the war. In order to reorganise the authorities and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that but my question is really very, very simple. Article 2 simply says that the executive committee has got to carry out preparations for the transition to work under wartime conditions. Now that's a really serious task, isn't it? A serious task for the -- and solemn and weighty task for the executive council, isn't it? Just answer "yes" or "no". It's a fairly simple question. I'm not asking for a history of the document. All I'm asking is that that's a serious topic, a serious matter that the executive council had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say to you that whoever wrote this decision did not know that a war would break out. I don't know how this kind of an article could have been written any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Di Fazio, please. Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fellow who signed the -- that or rather appends, attaches his name to this particular portion, Dusan Tanasac? Is there any reason to think that the chairman of the municipal assembly got this wrong, that he wrote down things in this Official Gazette that are incorrect?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Tanasac as far as I know did not take part in the elaboration of this Official Gazette. As far as I know this was done by Mitar Mitrovic, secretary of the municipal assembly. I don't know which archives he drew upon and what sources he used for writing this document, so Mitar Mitrovic is the one who should really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So let's be clear about this. Is your position that this document is not the Official Gazette of the municipality of Samac? Is that what you're saying to the Chamber? Feel free to say it if you wish but is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not what I'm saying. I'm talking about the technology of writing this. I'm talking about the shortcomings. I'm putting the following question. On the basis of which information, which data, was this Official Gazette compiled, since it was published in June, 1994, that is to say two years after the event that we are discussing right now. The author of this gazette, did he have all the relevant information for compiling it? I doubt it. I'm not challenging the fact that this is the Official Gazette. That is not something that I'm challenging before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're saying that it's inaccurate. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was inaccurate. I have been saying the following. I have put a question. Did the author have enough information to compile this Official Gazette two years later? Because from a legal point of view, there are certain shortcomings, and you also said that this Official Gazette was a bit strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Ninkovic just for the sake of clarity, you mention that as far as you knew the gazette was done, to use the words of the transcript by Mitar Mitrovic, secretary of the municipal assembly. I presume that this is the same Mitar Mitrovic who signed Exhibit D55/1, which is the list of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Samac on which your name appears as a member of the Crisis Staff. It is the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to what I believe is paragraph 6 of the gazette, headed, "Decision to confirm (verify) the decisions and other legislation of the war president [sic] of the Samac municipal assembly" and there follows a list of various decisions that were confirmed. Can you find that? It follows a few pages later.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is precisely the page I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just intervention to the transcript. It's page 19, line 15, said war president, which is not in consistency with what my learned friend just has said, I think. He mentioned War Presidency, not war president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. It will be corrected. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found that article, that decision, article?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the page where all the decisions are. Could you please repeat the decision that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to find the portion of the gazette. Now, what --

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. And it says that essentially it says this, between the 17th of April, 1992 and January, 1993, various decisions were confirmed and they list them out there, going all the way to 38 of them. Go to number ten. "Decision on the executive council and administrative bodies." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to repeat before this Trial Chamber that I'm not challenging the Official Gazette as a public gazette issued by the local authorities. I'm talking about the technology according to which this Official Gazette was compiled. The municipal assembly on that date -- I mean it verified the decisions of the Crisis Staff, and I'm not challenging that either. But now, when I look at item 10, I'm not challenging that that was verified too, but I am expressing my doubts as regards the following: Whether what was actually happening was translated into these decisions in the right way, whether the text accurately reflects what was actually happening. So I think that from a legal and professional point of view, I think that there were certain shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, let's perhaps approach it from another -- another angle to see if this executive board is actually functioning or not. If Your Honours please, page 20 of the English. I'd like you, please, to go to again I believe it's paragraph 12 of the gazette. It deals with notice of appointment of senior official in the administration, signed Mirko Jovanovic, president of the executive council. It's towards the end of the document. Can you find that, please?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a few decisions here. On the election of the Presidency of the municipal assembly, the vice-president, the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the one that appoints Milan Simic to assistant secretary of the municipal secretariat for the economy. Do you find that? Paragraph 12 and it's dated the 15th of April, 1992. Do you --

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found that yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just --

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's after the decision on the executive council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It follows on from that. It's after that. It's -- it's preceded immediately by a notice to dismiss Ilija Ristic, and then it follows immediately after, all right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. I found it. Yes. This is the decision on appointing the management organs, members of the -- that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, it says in the preamble, that a session was held on the 15th of April, 1992, and that the executive council made this decision appointing Milan Simic. Now that would indicate that this executive board or executive council was up and running and leading an active, happy existence, wouldn't it? Actually working, functioning, meeting, carrying on its business?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that I have no information that the executive council had a meeting. I don't have any information about anybody informing me that the council had any such meeting. I am very decisive in telling you this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Very well. If that's your position, that's your position. However, you would agree with me that as a matter of simple, pure logic, it must indicate that an executive council was functioning midway -- in fact two days before the outbreak of hostilities in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we used logic in the sense of interpreting this document, the decision provides the answer, but I am telling you that the council was not operative, and perhaps it's possible that somebody made a mistake with the date when compiling this report two years later, this gazette. What I know is that the executive council was really working when Milan Simic was placed as the President of the executive council, and when Mirko Lukic was his deputy. That executive council did work. This is not something that I am disputing. This is beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, if Your Honours just bear with me, my microphone is acting up, can I just switch over to the other one, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, one other matter that I want to ask you about that arises from this document. Please continue into the next paragraph, which is paragraph 13. Now, there you see another decision of the executive council taken on the 14th. That is the day before the appointment of Milan Simic. Do you see that decision? Or conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to ask you if there was an executive council functioning on the 14th. I understand now what your position is but I do want to ask you about one paragraph 3 of that -- of that conclusion. It says that the President of the executive council assigned the chief of public security station to form a special purpose unit of the MUP and attached to the public security station in collaboration with the responsible bodies of the military and civilian authorities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, the head of the public security station was Todorovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the eve of the war you're talking about, during the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the chief of -- he was the head of the public security station even before that, wasn't he? Didn't he -- he was appointed in February, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You need to look in the personnel files, when the Minister of Internal Affairs appointed Todorovic as the chief of the public security station. That is the only thing that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm actually interested in is this: Have you got any idea what this special purpose unit was, who was in it, what its job was? What special purposes it dealt with?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about such a unit existing at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears on paper that this special purpose unit was to act in conjunction with the civilian authorities and the military. Now, isn't that a matter that would have concerned the Ministry of Defence, in which you were carrying out duties?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an inconsistent text that has no basis in the facts, if we are talking about the wartime period, there was a unit for special purposes in the Republika Srpska MUP, but it was under the authority of the Minister of Internal Affairs, and it did not operate in the territory of the municipality of Samac and that has nothing to do with what it says here. I don't know about any MUP units in the territory of the Samac municipality prior to the break out of the war or during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The executive council obviously thought that they could tell the chief of public security station to form such a unit and they decided to do that on the 14th. Now, they still operating under that notion the following day on the 15th, because the next article deals with the same topic. If you go to paragraph 3, paragraph 3, of -- sorry, yes, paragraph 3 of paragraph 14, the second-to-last paragraph, and it says that the special purpose unit has got to -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, again, I assume you can't tell us anything about this special purposes unit. You don't know anything about it or its existence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no special purpose unit prior to the break out of the war or during the war in the municipality of Samac, particularly not in connection with the public security station, as far as I know. So this item 2 [as interpreted] in this text is empty. It has no content, as far as I know, first of all the term Serbian Territorial Defence, it did not exist. There was only the Yugoslav People's Army as the only legal armed structure. So that this term to me is something to be disputed. What I want to say is that this item 3 is just empty words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you allow me just as a matter of clarification, I heard when the witness said this is at page 25, line 1, that he said item 3 instead of item 2, which is in the transcript, so I kindly ask this correction because afterwards, he also mentioned item 3 in this part of his testimony, so there is some inconsistency between these two issues, item 2 and item 3, maybe my learned friend can clarify that. I think it's just an error in the transcript. MR. DI FAZIO: Obviously just an error in the transcript if Your Honours please, I'm certain that the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm only talking about item 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suppose given what you've told us about this special purpose unit, you could not possibly explain why immediate steps had to be taken to form this unit on the 15th of April? You would have no idea about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you would disagree that it was in preparation for an imminent takeover on the night of the 16th and 17th of April by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this qualification about the takeover of power does not stand, according to me it's not a term that could be applied to the situation in Samac. When we are talking about that night between the 16th and the 17th, when the regular armed forces from the legal Yugoslav People's Army prevented and thwarted an attack by regular forces from the Republic of Croatia and the paramilitary forces from Samac itself and its environs and that is my precise definition of that night, that date, and that event. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness just be shown Exhibit P126, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The preamble to this document is what I'm interested in. In fact the very first few lines. You see that it refers to an operation for the liberation of Bosanski Samac and the creation of the first free Serbian municipality started during the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This preamble was written in June of 1993 by Dr. Blagoje Simic. You can check that for yourself by just going to the end of the preamble.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wonder about the use of the language there, it says an operation for the liberation of Bosanski Samac started that night. I assume Bosanski Samac hadn't yet been taken over by Croatian forces or any other forces by that stage, by the 16th and 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to state my position. You will find in many documents which have been presented before this Chamber different terms and concepts which are simply not authentic. They are simply not based on the regulations or they simply do not stand, and this is a reflection of people who were not qualified but who compiled this -- these documents. You will find such bad qualifications, imprecisions and so on. Many documents were written by people who, let me say, did not know, did not have much experience in their job, were not trained, did not have the information required so they used terms which were inadequate. I believe that this part also that you are talking about came from such a mental state so from someone who was not knowledgeable enough to use the proper term, the Yugoslav People's Army had intelligence data that an attack on Samac was being prepared from the Republic of Croatia assisted by forces from within Samac and its environs. Some members of the army could testify about this who saw a column of tanks immediately across the Sava River on the 17th in the morning, from -- how come that there was a column of tanks or several tanks on the 17th of April in the morning just in front of the bridge towards Samac? Were they there by chance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your position. I'm not trying to contradict you on that. I don't accept it but I understand what your position is. But I'm more interested in the language that was used here. You say there was an unfortunate lack of precision in the language. That couldn't have applied to Dr. Blagoje Simic. First of all, he was an educated man. He was a doctor. Secondly, he had by the time he wrote this, had some considerable experience in administration. This is written in June of 1993. He'd been president of the Crisis Staff, the War Presidency, the municipal assembly. And thirdly, he's writing in a document that demands precision. It's a gazette. So all of those factors combined would really make sure that he chose his words carefully, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, Dr. Blagoje Simic, he would sign documents prepared by others, and as far as I know, he was not very diligent in reading the actual text of the document beforehand. Blagoje Simic is a doctor, but I am not sure whether doctors know other things as well as they know medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That might be so but the other curious aspect of the first sentence that he uses is this: He refers to an operation, A for the liberation of Bosanski Samac, and secondly, for the creation of the first free Serbian municipality. Do you know anything about that? What -- what was this operation to create the first free Serb municipality? Can you tell the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment on that, if we take the region from the River Tinja which is west of Brcko about six or seven kilometres, up to Prnjavor which is another 120 kilometres to the west and if we take the depth of the territory from the River Sava, from the border with Croatia some 25 to 30 kilometres, the region of the municipality of Samac itself was not under the control of the army of Republic of Croatia or the HVO so it was just the municipality of Samac so this is probably in that sense. So this area is 120 by 25 kilometres. It's a pretty large area. At that point, the municipality of Samac, which was controlled by the Serb forces was spread over an area of about 170 kilometres. All the other municipalities, Bosanski Brod, Derventa are part of the Doboj municipality; Modrica, Odzak a part of the Bosanski Samac municipality; Orasje, Gradacac a part of the Brcko municipality, was held by the armed formations of the Republic of Croatia and the HVO, and the Muslim paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I suggest to you that the interpretation that you've given is -- strains credibility to the breaking point. I suggest to you there Dr. Blagoje Simic is speaking with commendable frankness and that he's talking the truth. Namely that the operation on the night of the 16th and 17th of April was in fact designed to create a Serbian municipality.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're practically talking about the existence of a preconceived plan for that. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. You hit it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I understand your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, another clarification, it's page 28, line 24, it says 170 kilometres, I don't believe that this witness said that the territory or region controlled by Serb forces is one. Could you clarify that? I mean it's something which we not heard. Page 28, line 24. It says about 170 kilometres, but we heard something else. Maybe you can clarify that. It's also an error in transcript which is important. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think there was a problem in transcript. You were talking about the area under control by Serb forces and you referred to a figure of 170 kilometres. Is that the figure that you actually mentioned, 170, or did you mention some other figure?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the size of the territory, 120 kilometres by 25 kilometres, which was controlled by the Croatian armed forces. Within that territory, there was about 170 kilometres, which, let me say, was controlled by the JNA at that point, if that's what the point of time we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn to another topic now. Do you know who was on the Crisis Staff in the first few months following the night of the 15th and 16th of April? Now you don't have to mention the ones we already do know but if you know the remainder. We know that Dr. Blagoje Simic was president, we know Mr. Tadic was on the Crisis Staff. Do you know of anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will list several more that I know about, although I don't know the final list, and I don't know whether this list was ever precisely defined. So Blagoje Simic, Simo -- no excuse me, Tadic, Miroslav; Simeon Simic, then Savo Popovic, then Fadil Topcagic, Mirko Jovanovic but I'm not quite sure about Mirko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the ensuing months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me just one question. What about Mr. Mitar Mitrovic that we are hearing a lot about? Was he on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what to say. He was a close associate of Blagoje Simic, who wrote, as far as I know, the majority of these decisions, and regulations. I don't have information about him being a member of the Crisis Staff. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that he could have been on the Crisis Staff but you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Milos Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff either. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit D55/1, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO for the benefit of our clients so that they know what we are talking about? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's just remind the Trial Chamber about yourself. Your position is that you were not and never were on the Crisis Staff. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell the Chamber why your name is there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that this was a -- because of the salary list, so that -- the payroll so that they would not put my name on it there. I was in the information service which was formed in order to disseminate information and Simeon Simic was a member of the Crisis Staff in charge of information. Because if you pursue that logic, there are also on this list the cook, security personnel, and they were not members of the Crisis Staff for sure, but they did need to be paid, to receive their salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I think it's important to explain to the witness that it's not a question of logic. The Trial Chamber wants facts. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you. I'll endeavour to do that, if Your Honours please. But perhaps before I do that, it's quarter to 4.00. Is now the time you intend to take the break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break and continue at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, continue. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, before I do continue, can I just ask you to indicate your views about time? I'm mindful of the fact that on the last occasion before Christmas you took the view that I should have a further three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I've used up one and a half of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm fearful that I won't be able to finish my cross-examination in the next one and a half hours and I'd like a bit more time. I'm doing the best I can. My assessment is that I will finish possibly, although unlikely, if I were allowed to proceed in the way I've devised my cross-examination, I would finish possibly later towards the end of the day, more likely fairly soon tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Di Fazio, you've had quite a long time for cross-examination and -- MR. DI FAZIO: I appreciate that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And the Trial Chamber sometimes notices repetition so you should wind up within the time allocated. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I appreciate that. I understand that, your view, I make no bones about that. I understand that fully, if Your Honour's please. But what I'm saying is that in order to complete I need a bit more time. And I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You start, we'll see how we go. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you if we could approach it in that ad hoc fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour if I may be of assistance with this matter? I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that Defence has another witness here but not in the premises. So it's more likely that it will be very complicated for us to arrange his presence here, because we plan to have him tomorrow morning, so in that sense maybe my learned friend can be more relaxed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How long will your re-examination take?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Re-examination, frankly, Your Honour, it's hard to say, 40, 30 minutes, 40 minutes maximum, more or less, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we could be quite within the time frame. Yes, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you if Your Honours please and I will endeavour to get through my cross-examination as swiftly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sorry we just want to ask the technical people, the laptop for Judge Williams is not working. You can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, we showed you D55/1, and you gave an explanation about the reason your name appears on D55. Do you know if any of the names listed under security were in fact simple -- were in fact simply guards or security officials?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were ordinary guards, and drivers at the same time, as far as I know, Branko Jokic, Milos Ilic, they worked as drivers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any reason to doubt that there would be other documents, if this is a valid and authentic document, that there would be other such documents dealing for June, July, the rest of the year?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document related to the salaries of persons who are on this list, possibly such a document exists. That is to say for the following month or I don't know, but I am not aware of any such document. I mean, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Blagoje Simic gave evidence in this case and he looked at this document and explained what it was about, and said that people who were named on it were in fact members of the Crisis Staff. Do you have any idea why he would say that and thereby include you as a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, objection. I don't -- well, I try to refresh my memory but I'm quite sure that my client didn't say that in that sense that all these people, including drivers and guards and the other stuff, are the members, including of course Mr. Ninkovic. MR. DI FAZIO: Page 12243 of the transcript he said that, however I'm even making allowances that it was a blanket statement and that it doesn't include the security guards and the cook, he didn't mean to include the security guards and the cook. So perhaps if I rephrase my question just to make sure that they are excluded and I'll -- so perhaps if I put the question to the witness again so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You do have the answer which Dr. Blagoje Simic gave. Why don't you just recite it? MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question by Mr. Pantelic: And does this list in fact reflect the situation and the membership of the Crisis Staff in April of 1992 when according to you it started functioning? Answer: Yes, it does. Simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I don't want you to speculate but I ask you this: Do you know of any reason why he would adopt that position? Because of course that includes you as a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Blagoje Simic fully understood the question, then I'm surprised by this answer which includes me as well. I will repeat that I was in the information service, I was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I have been repeating that several times now so there is no need for me to repeat it yet again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. We are both -- we both understand each other perfectly well but I do want to persist with this topic because you may be able to assist us. Still on the same topic, is the -- is utterances made by Mr. Tadic in the past, he was interviewed by officers of the Office of the Prosecutor in March of 1998, and when he was interviewed regarding membership of the Crisis Staff, he said that Milos Bogdanovic was on the Crisis Staff by virtue of his being chief of the secretariat of national defence. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. There was no functional appointment, as far as I know, related to membership on the Crisis Staff. This is probably a position taken by Mr. Tadic that was a bit arbitrary, although I will say to you, as far as I know, there was a large number of people there who participated in meetings, who came and went, so I would not look at this Crisis Staff as a precisely defined body with certain powers. It was a rather broad-based organ in which many people who had certain tasks came, presented their positions, presented certain problems, took part in a discussion that would relate to the problem -- to the matters that they were in charge of. So I would not attach such importance to the Crisis Staff. It had quite a few forms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I do attach importance to the Crisis Staff, and I'd like to know, as precisely as possible, who was on it and who was not. You say it had quite a few forms. Do you mean that its membership was fluid and people would join at sometimes and others would leave at other times? Its membership was fluctuating? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is not my position. I want to say that people came to these meetings, depending on the problems that were on the agenda, and that not always the same people were present at each and every session, so there were many more people than those who are on this list that were involved in a certain way in the process of making certain decisions, if I can put it that way or information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For you to explain this, you presumably must have been present often at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you that there were two telephones that were accessible to me so that I could do my work as a journalist. That was the telephone attached to the Crisis Staff and the telephone at the reporting centre. So when I was in the premises where the Crisis Staff was inter alia, there were several offices, different people came there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about telephones, I'm asking you about your presence at meetings. You've described -- you've described a lot of different people coming along to these meetings and this would happen quite often. Now, for you to give that evidence, for you to be able to tell us that that's in fact what happened, as a matter of reason, you must have been there often yourself, often at Crisis Staff meetings, in order to describe this. Otherwise it wouldn't be possible, correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was often at the premises of the Crisis Staff, but I was not often at sessions of the Crisis Staff. These are two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that for to you carry out your duties at the Ministry of Defence it would have been very important for you to know who was in the leadership of the -- of the municipality and who was in the Crisis Staff, since it was the highest civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that question, I am going to give the following answer: When I was there, I don't know, I was there very little, names were not called out, and there was no calling out of names in the sense of who was there, who was not there. That's not the way meetings would begin. The agenda would be discussed. Problems that were on the agenda. That was probably a technology of work about which Blagoje Simic could say more than I could. He convened these meetings so how did he convene them, in which way, according to which list?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can the witness be shown P72? While P72 -- whilst that document is being obtained, can I ask you this? You agree that the notion of work obligation that you've testified about is a type of war assignment? That's in effect the evidence that you gave?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for work obligation, it has to be carried out, that is clearly sanctioned, because that would mean a violation of law in wartime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree that it's a type of war assignment, not whether it has to be carried out. You agree it's a type of war assignment. I can take you back to your own words if you wish, if you'd like me to remind you what you said on the last occasion, I will, otherwise I pose the question simply, war obligation is a type of war assignment. Do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not quite literally, because who -- those who had work obligation were not members of a military formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me --

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, this needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not seeking clarification because I suggest that you abundantly clear when answering questions by Mr. Pantelic, page 13477. Question: If I understood you correctly, work obligation is also a type of war assignment? Answer: Yes, it is. Question: You explained that before. Answer: Yes, and the command of the military unit does not have the right to change anybody's war assignment. He is not in a position to do so. All right, now I've refreshed your memory and that's what your position is -- was, work obligation is a type of war assignment, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Absolutely, work obligation is war assignment. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with the proposition that the -- that work obligation as a war assignment exists for the defence of the nation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree that the Serb forces, would it be your position that the Serb forces in Bosanski Samac were fighting a war of self defence from aggression? They were not aggressors? That would have to be your position, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P72, just let's have a look at that. Now, this is a gazette dated 8th of June, 1992, and it's been signed apparently or rather the author of the document, of the gazette, is apparently Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it -- the effect of the document is to form War Presidencies in municipalities, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This decision pertains to that subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Article 3 says that "A War Presidency is to organise, coordinate and adjust activities for the defence of the Serbian people, and in addition establish lawful municipal authorities." Article 3, first paragraph or sentence?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also third sentence, "It's also got to create and ensure the conditions for the work of military bodies and units in defending the Serbian nation," okay?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of logic, then, War Presidencies have to work with the Ministry of Defence, since work obligation is part of the defence of the nation. That's reasonable, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would be therefore of supreme importance that the Ministry of Defence work very, very closely with the Crisis Staff, or War Presidency as it was later known? In view of this gazette.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that in that part, the executive council did a lot more direct work, made decisions, et cetera. I think that that can be seen from the documentation involved because the executive board had very serious obligations in the sphere of the economy. So the cooperation was greater with the executive council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe so but I'm not asking you about the executive council. I'm asking you about the Ministry of Defence. If the Ministry of Defence is responsible for work obligation, if work obligation is part of the defence of the nation, then according to this gazette, it makes sense that the Ministry of Defence, who are responsible for dealing with work obligation, work hand in glove, very closely with the War Presidency. That's demanded by Article 3, isn't it? It's required by Article 3, because work obligation is defence --

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your interpretation of this decision. As for this task regarding work obligation, we had the law, the order of the Minister of Defence. We had the executive council. I am not disputing that the Crisis Staff in principle had this position, but in direct terms, it did not have, how should I put this, it was not directly involved with regard to this matter in that period. Later, in 1995, when a state of war was declared, according to law, the War Presidencies then ratified wartime job descriptions, et cetera, but this was later. This was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about 1995. I'm asking you about 1992, 1992. It's simplicity itself, is it not? Look, you've said twice that work obligation is a matter of defence of the nation. You said it in your examination-in-chief, in answer to questions by Mr. Pantelic. You reaffirmed it today when I asked you, and we know that your department, Ministry of Defence, was the very body that oversaw, organised, work obligation. Now, if work obligation is a form of defence, then Article 3 of this gazette demands, requires, that the War Presidency organise, coordinate, adjust activities for the defence of the Serbian people, as a matter of logic, you, the Ministry of Defence and the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency must have worked together for this to be effectively adhered to, followed, the orders of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, sorry, the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia. How can it be any other way?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me for my comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because you were working for the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, may I say that the ministry is in charge of allocation. However, your position that we oversaw this, this is a matter that can be discussed item by item because you put it in too strong terms. There was the executive council, then the director of the enterprise -- of the company where a person worked, et cetera, but I claim as regards work obligation, it was not indispensable to have this kind of cooperation that you are referring to, namely between the department of the Ministry of Defence and the Crisis Staff. Functionally, it was more important between the department of the Ministry of Defence and the executive council, or -- because the executive council saw how the economy was functioning, and they needed the labour force involved. They could see how many people were needed. The Crisis Staff did not have such tasks. Perhaps something can be drawn out of this decision, along these lines, but that's not the way it was in practice. Furthermore, the date here is the 31st of May. At that time I wasn't in the ministry yet. It was only on the 16th of July that I was appointed head of the department of the Ministry of Defence, and I testified about that last time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the reason I asked you about this is simply to put to you so that you understand my position, the Prosecution's position, that according to P72, the Official Gazette, it really, as I've already said to you twice now, demanded that you work hand in glove -- sorry, that the Crisis Staff work hand in glove with the Ministry of Defence because work obligation is a type of defence, and that if that is so, it would make absolute sense for someone from the Ministry of Defence to be on the Crisis Staff, to be a member of the Crisis Staff, because it's such an important function. That's what I was driving at. Now, would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to accept your conclusions as my own position? Your interpretations of this? I can't accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You don't have to but I want you to understand --

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been trying all this time, no, I understand this full well. Now you're trying to construct something on the basis of this Article 3 and you want me just to say "yes" and I have been explaining all the time that it was not indispensable to have this kind of firm direct cooperation between the department of the ministry and the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff is an organ which was not involved in immediate executive work, if I can put it that way. In that section the Crisis Staff did not have this direct engagement. This can be seen on the basis of some decisions that were made on -- by the executive council, like on war production, et cetera. There are some decisions that are far more important than the one we are looking at right now and that speak about these relations. I discussed them in detail during my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And just to end this topic of membership of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Simo Zaric was interviewed -- if Your Honour will just bear with me, please, for one moment? Was interviewed twice in I think 1998, regarding events in Bosanski Samac. The 2nd of April, 1998, my learned friends will find this at P141 and 142. He was asked about membership of the Crisis Staff and yourself, and he said that you were a member of the Crisis Staff on both occasions. Now, again, I am not inviting you to speculate as to what was in his mind but if you do know of any reason or can think of any solid reason as to why he would adopt the view that you were on the Crisis Staff, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his motives are, but as far as I know, Mr. Zaric, he liked to promote himself in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Okay. But this was -- I understand what you say but this was not a media interview. This was an interview with -- I should be-- I'm sorry if I misled you. This was an interview with officers of the Office of the Prosecutor who was being interviewed following his arrest and he said that you were on the Crisis Staff, twice, two separate interviews. Now, if you know of any reason why he would say that, tell us.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't finish. I don't know what were the reasons for which he said that, but I know that many of his statements were untrue, just like that one. Not only that one is untrue but other ones too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
